content: Dr. James O. Mason, the Director of the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) in 1984, issued a challenge to the public health community to devise a comprehensive strategy aimed at eradicating tuberculosis (TB) in the United States. This initiative led to the development of a detailed plan by the CDC and the Department of Health and Human Services' Advisory Committee for the Elimination of Tuberculosis. Numerous experts, both internal and external to the department, contributed significantly to the creation of this plan, and their efforts are deeply appreciated. The plan has garnered support from key organizations, including the American Medical Association's House of Delegates, the Governing Council of the American Public Health Association, the American Lung Association, and the American College of Preventive Medicine. These endorsements reflect a shared commitment to the goal of eliminating TB, and it is anticipated that other organizations will follow suit in the near future. The public health community must collectively commit to this objective and actively promote it to encourage widespread participation in this critical effort. The CDC is currently identifying both short-term and long-term activities to implement the plan effectively. The plan is being disseminated to a broad range of public and private organizations with recommendations for similar actions. The Department of Health and Human Services has also established an Advisory Committee for the Elimination of Tuberculosis to provide guidance on developing new technologies, applying prevention and control methods, and managing state and local TB programs aimed at eradicating the disease as a public health issue. The plan outlines a realistic goal of reducing TB incidence to 5 cases per 100,000 population by the year 2000, with further reduction to 3 cases per 100,000 as a subsequent target. This goal is achievable due to three key factors: the geographic and demographic concentration of TB cases into defined pockets, advancements in biotechnology that enable improved diagnostic, treatment, and prevention methods, and the potential of modern technologies such as computers and telecommunications to enhance the transfer of these innovations into practice. A three-step action plan has been developed to achieve these goals: 1. Optimizing the use of existing prevention and control methods, particularly in high-risk populations. 2. Developing and evaluating new technologies for TB treatment, diagnosis, and prevention. 3. Rapidly assessing and integrating newly developed technologies into clinical and public health practices. The committee emphasizes the importance of engaging the medical community and the public in constructive discussions and actions to raise awareness about TB and foster a collective commitment to its elimination. Despite significant progress in TB control, the disease remains a public health concern in the United States, with isolated and potentially dangerous enclaves of infection persisting. Without more aggressive action, preventable cases and deaths will continue to occur well into the next century. Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria from the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, which are typically transmitted through airborne particles when an infected individual with respiratory TB coughs. Inhalation of these bacteria can lead to infection, which may spread throughout the body. While most infected individuals do not develop clinical illness due to immune system control, they remain at risk of disease progression, particularly if their immune system becomes compromised. TB primarily affects the lungs but can occur in virtually any part of the body. The ongoing analysis of TB morbidity data highlights the magnitude and extent of the problem, providing critical insights for control and elimination efforts. Between 1953 and 1984, the number of reported TB cases decreased by an average of 5% annually. However, this trend reversed in the mid-1980s, partly due to the emergence of TB among individuals infected with HIV, which causes immunosuppression and allows latent TB infections to progress to active disease. Consequently, TB screening and prevention efforts must prioritize individuals with or at risk for HIV infection. Although TB case rates have declined across all racial groups over the past two decades, the decrease has been less pronounced among nonwhite populations. Currently, nearly two-thirds of TB cases occur among Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Native American individuals. The higher risk in these minority populations is likely linked to socioeconomic factors such as inadequate housing and nutrition. Prevention and control strategies must be tailored to address the specific needs of these high-risk groups. TB is also prevalent among immigrants, refugees, and migrant workers from countries with high disease prevalence. In these populations, drug-resistant TB strains, particularly those resistant to isoniazid (INH), are more common. If not properly managed, drug-resistant TB can lead to treatment failure and further transmission. Specific control efforts should target recent immigrants, particularly within the first two years of their arrival in the United States, as this is when nearly half of TB cases among immigrant Asians occur. Screening and preventive measures should be implemented before or shortly after their arrival. Among all racial and ethnic groups, TB case rates are highest among the elderly, with the majority of cases occurring in community-dwelling seniors rather than those in nursing homes. Effective epidemiologic surveillance is essential for targeting high-risk populations and geographic areas, as well as for designing and evaluating prevention and control programs. The first step in the action plan focuses on improving the use of existing prevention and control methods. This includes ensuring adequate treatment for all TB patients, identifying high-risk population groups, and implementing preventive treatment for appropriate individuals. Surveillance, disease prevention, containment, and program evaluation are key components of this strategy. Improving surveillance involves timely identification and reporting of TB cases, suspected cases, and contacts. Health departments should establish systems to ensure that individuals with TB symptoms receive diagnostic evaluations within two weeks of initial contact with a healthcare provider. Suspected or diagnosed cases should be reported to health departments within three days to facilitate contact investigations and preventive interventions. Preventable TB cases continue to occur in the United States, often due to missed opportunities for intervention. These include contact identification and examination, preventive therapy for latent infections, prompt diagnosis and reporting, and adequate ventilation in high-risk facilities. Preventive therapy with INH can reduce the risk of TB by over 90% among individuals who complete the full course of treatment. Efforts to improve disease containment should ensure that all TB patients complete an appropriate course of therapy. Health departments should assign specific staff to oversee patient education, continuity of therapy, and contact investigations. Incentives and directly observed therapy may be necessary to enhance treatment adherence, particularly for high-risk populations. Program assessment and evaluation are critical for ensuring the effectiveness and efficiency of TB control efforts. Health departments should annually evaluate their progress toward TB elimination, including analyses of morbidity and mortality data, case reporting, and prevention activities. Collaboration with organizations such as lung associations and professional societies is encouraged to share information and improve program performance. The implementation of this plan requires strong commitment at all levels—national, state, and community. Advisory groups with broad representation should develop and implement strategies tailored to the needs of their respective communities. The ultimate goal is to achieve a TB-free society through coordinated and sustained efforts.
